title: David Choe Kayfabe care-package inventory
summary: Jim Rugg and Ed Piskor inventory and divide a David Choe care package containing Slow Jams, Dirty Hands, Bruised Fruit, Mangchi zines, Giant Robot and Juxtapoz material, DC covers, Soothsayers, Snowman Monkey BBQ and other ephemera. The record separates visible objects, withheld interiors, host memory, material guesses, rarity/value jokes, private custody, DVDASA recap, unrelated weekly discussion and long dated commerce.

quality.assessment: Complete chronological read. The Choe package is bounded from unrelated weekly-show and commerce material; object/title/name damage is repaired, uncertain works remain unresolved, masked words remain masked.

speaker_policy: Public hosts are Jim Rugg and Ed Piskor, but captions have no publisher names. Publish zero named turns pending held-out validation.

connections.relationship: A private care package becomes a visible but incomplete inventory of Choe's print output.
Choe's warning and hosts' restraint show that possession does not authorize broadcasting interiors.
The gift reconnects the hosts' formative 1999 discovery with Choe's later relationship to the channel.
The DVD package adds bonus-feature evidence beyond the documentary itself.
A possible hair-pull technique is interesting precisely because the hosts label their uncertainty.
The object connects Choe's early writing voice to an art-book format after Slow Jams.
A drawing collection locates Choe inside Giant Robot's publishing ecosystem.
Edition claims and million-dollar jokes show how collector excitement can outrun verification.
DC variants show Choe's image-making inside corporate character systems.
Anthology credits link Choe with Jordan Crane, James Jean and other makers.
Opening the object yields a 2013 date that corrects vague recency memory.
Coin flips document division but do not establish future ownership or archive access.
Bonus-feature names prompt a separate, unverified recap of recurring podcast participants.
Covers, zines, magazines and DVDs collectively reveal breadth that a painting-only biography misses.
The Choe inventory ends well before the episode, preventing unrelated weekly talk from entering his biography.
Ross discussion contrasts comics autonomy with advertising and film collaboration.
Hosts' no-downtime thesis is preserved as opinion rather than creator-health guidance.
A long dated outro documents channel economics but not current availability.
